Orphaned of his murdered father at age two, this Shia cleric grew up to lead a revolution that toppled the Shah and made him his country's first supreme leader — who was he?
Ruhollah Khomeini: Supreme Leader of Iran from 1979 to 1989.
This French economist and Green party lawmaker, representing a Paris constituency since 2022, became a leading voice of France's version of the Me Too movement — who is she?
Sandrine Rousseau: French economist and politician. Rousseau previously served as a vice-president of the University of Lille.

A close confidant of Vladimir Putin, this Russian official ran the Emergency Situations ministry for two decades before serving as Defence Minister and being tasked with supervising the war in Ukraine — who is he?
This king moved Poland's capital from Kraków to Warsaw and was the first Polish monarch from a Swedish royal house — who is he?
Sigismund III Vasa: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania (1587–1632), King of Sweden (1592–1599)

He out-debated and beat Abraham Lincoln for an 1858 Senate seat, then lost to him for the presidency two years later — and helped broker the Compromise of 1850 along the way. Which Illinois Democrat was he?
Stephen A. Douglas: American politician and lawyer (1813–1861)
Born in Doha in 1980, this man only became heir after an older brother renounced the throne — and he's reigned over his Gulf nation since 2013. Who is he?
Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani: Emir of Qatar since 2013.
At just 33, this Marxist revolutionary became president after a coup staged on his behalf, then launched sweeping reforms he called the people's democratic revolution — who is he?
Thomas Sankara: President of Burkina Faso from 1983 to 1987.
Dubbed 'the Nelson of the East' by Western reporters, this Imperial Japanese Navy admiral penned Russia's fleet into Port Arthur before a decisive 1905 victory at Tsushima — who is he?

Spanning roughly 800 to 1050 CE, this era of Norse raiding, trading, and settlement saw Scandinavians reach as far as Newfoundland, becoming the first Europeans known to set foot in North America. What period was this?
Viking Age: Period of European history (about 800–1050)
Fought from December 1812 to May 1814, this multinational alliance of European powers finally defeated Napoleon's empire and forced him into exile on Elba — which conflict?
War of the Sixth Coalition: 1813–1814 conflict during the Napoleonic Wars.
Commander of the Indonesian Armed Forces during the country's 1998 transition from authoritarian rule, this retired general later chaired the Presidential Advisory Council — who is it?
Wiranto: Indonesian general and politician. On 27 July 2016, Wiranto was appointed Coordinating Minister for Political, Legal, and Security Affairs, replacing Luhut Binsar Panjaitan.
A graduate of Cairo University who briefly served as Japan's defense minister in 2007, this politician has governed Tokyo since 2016 — who is she?
Yuriko Koike: Governor of Tokyo since 2016. Yuriko Koike (Japanese: 小池 百合子, Hepburn: Koike Yuriko; born 15 July 1952) is a Japanese politician who has served as the Governor of Tokyo since 2016.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Ada Lovelace (born 1815) is the earliest of the four. Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer.
Who among these was born first?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was born first?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these came out first?
MUMPS (published 1966) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Alessandro Volta is a physicist. Throughout his life, Volta enjoyed a certain amount of closeness with the emperor who conferred upon him numerous honours.
Which of these four is a chemist?
Samuel Conway is a chemist. Samuel Charles Conway (born June 4, 1965) is an American researcher in the pharmaceutical, biomedical and agrochemical fields of organic chemistry.
What is the atomic number of Lithium?
Lithium (from Ancient Greek: λίθος, líthos, 'stone') is a chemical element; it has symbol Li and atomic number 3.
In what year was Blaise Pascal born?
Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 – 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
In what year was Friedrich Engels born?
Friedrich Engels: After Marx's death, Engels served as the editor of his works, completing the second and third volumes of Das Kapital.
In what year was Edward Teller born?
Edward Teller: Born in Austria-Hungary in 1908, Teller emigrated to the US in the 1930s, one of the many so-called "Martians", a group of Hungarian scientist émigrés.
In what year did J. Robert Oppenheimer die?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: In 1941, Oppenheimer was briefed about nuclear weapon design by Australian physicist Mark Oliphant.
In what year did Kitty Oppenheimer die?
Kitty Oppenheimer: Robert Oppenheimer, the director of the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos Laboratory during World War II.
In what year was Fructose discovered?
Fructose, or fruit sugar, is a common monosaccharide, i.e. a simple sugar.
In what year was Gallium discovered?
Gallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ga and atomic number 31.
Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control
Lorazepam: Pfizer. Lorazepam, sold under the brand name Ativan among others, is a benzodiazepine medication.
Which country is AIDC F-CK-1 Ching-kuo from?
AIDC F-CK-1 Ching-kuo: Taiwan. The aircraft made its first flight in 1989.
Who is credited with discovering Plutonium?
Plutonium: Glenn Theodore Seaborg. Plutonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pu and atomic number 94.
Who is credited with discovering Fermium?
Fermium: Glenn Theodore Seaborg. Fermium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fm and atomic number 100.
Who is credited with discovering Sodium?
Sodium: Humphry Davy. Sodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Na (from Neo-Latin natrium) and atomic number 11.
Taken as a pill, cream, or injection, this antiviral medication is the go-to treatment for herpes simplex, chickenpox, and shingles — what is it?
Aciclovir is an antiviral medication. It is primarily used for the treatment of herpes simplex virus infections, chickenpox, and shingles.
This amphoteric compound forms a gelatinous precipitate in water and occurs naturally as the mineral gibbsite, one of bauxite's key components — what is it?
Aluminium hydroxide is a white chemical compound that is found as the mineral gibbsite (also known as hydrargillite) and its three much rarer polymorphs: bayerite, doyleite, and nordstrandite.
This scientific discipline bridges biology and sociology, studying human behavior, cultures, societies, and languages across time. What field is it?

Anthropology is the scientific study of humanity that crosses biology and sociology, concerned with human behavior, human biology, cultures, societies, and linguistics, in both the present and past, including archaic humans.
This common long-term inflammatory airway disease causes wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath that can flare into sudden attacks triggered by allergens or pollen. What condition is it?
Asthma is a common long-term inflammatory disease of the airways. It is characterized by variable and recurring symptoms and reduced lung function.
A civil-engineering graduate who first reshaped his father's firm toward real estate, this Frenchman now chairs the world's largest luxury goods company — who is he?
Bernard Arnault (born 5 March 1949) is a French businessman.
Every subatomic particle is either this integer-spin class or a fermion; Paul Dirac named the class after physicist Satyendra Nath Bose, whose statistics they obey — what's the class called?
Boson is a subatomic particle whose spin quantum number has an integer value (0, 1, 2,...).
Produced when quicklime is mixed with water, this white, powdery compound goes by many names in industry and food prep, where it's labeled E526 — what compound is it?
Calcium hydroxide (traditionally called slaked lime) is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula Ca(OH)2.
Retired from Istanbul Technical University, this geologist holds foreign membership in both the US and Russian National Academies of Sciences. Who is he?
Celâl Şengör (born 24 March 1955) is a Turkish geologist.

This genus of flowering trees and shrubs, native to South and East Asia, Melanesia, and Australia, gave rise through extensive hybridization to oranges, lemons, grapefruits, and limes — what's the genus called?
Citrus is a genus of flowering trees and shrubs in the family Rutaceae.

What zoological term describes the internal-fertilization mating behavior in which a male animal introduces sperm directly into a female's reproductive tract — occurring via a 'cloacal kiss' in birds and most reptiles, or vaginally in mammals?
Copulation (zoology) is animal sexual behavior in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body, especially directly into the female's reproductive tract.
This Canadian-born entrepreneur co-founded a company later acquired by MSC Software in 1998, then went on to co-found and lead a massively popular online gaming and creation platform — who is he?
David Baszucki (buh-; born January 20, 1963) is a Canadian-born American entrepreneur, engineer, and software developer.
This Penn professor's discoveries about modified nucleosides made the Pfizer and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines possible, earning him a share of the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine — who is he?
Drew Weissman (born September 7, 1959) is an American physician and immunologist known for his contributions to RNA biology.
This branch of medicine studies the body's hormone-secreting glands and the chemical messengers, called hormones, that regulate growth, metabolism, mood, and more — name the field?
Endocrinology (from endocrine + -ology) is a branch of biology and medicine dealing with the endocrine system, its diseases, and its specific secretions known as hormones.
Known for filling pillows and blankets as well as lining the wings of birds, what are these soft, complex integumentary structures called?
Feather are epidermal growths that form a distinctive outer covering, or plumage, on both avian (bird) and some non-avian dinosaurs and other archosaurs.

This American mechanical engineer and pioneering management consultant wrote a 1909 book that Academy of Management fellows later voted the most influential management book of the entire 20th century — who was he?
Frederick Winslow Taylor (March 20, 1856 - March 21, 1915) was an American mechanical engineer.

Encoded by the codons CAA and CAG and structurally related to glutamic acid but with an amide in place of a carboxylic acid group, this charge-neutral amino acid becomes essential under bodily stress — which amino acid?
Glutamine (symbol Gln or Q) is an -amino acid that is used in the biosynthesis of proteins.

This herbivorous mammal, the largest in its family of lagomorphs, nests in shallow ground depressions called 'forms' and is built for speed with long hind legs and heat-dissipating ears — what animal is it?
Hare are mammals belonging to the genus Lepus.
This American physicist threw out the wave-function collapse postulate, instead folding the observer into the same quantum state — an idea later known as the many-worlds interpretation. Who was he?
Hugh Everett III (November 11, 1930 - July 19, 1982) was an American physicist who proposed the relative state interpretation of quantum mechanics.
Patented in 1961 and approved two years later, this nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug works by blocking the enzyme cyclooxygenase to cut prostaglandin production — what drug is it?
Indometacin is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) commonly used as a prescription medication to reduce fever, pain, stiffness, and swelling from inflammation.
Born in Albuquerque and a Princeton engineering graduate, this businessman founded and once ran Amazon, the e-commerce and cloud-computing giant — who is he?

Jeff Bezos (n Jorgensen; born January 12, 1964) is an American businessman, and the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon, the world's largest e-commerce and cloud computing company.
Also called a kilopond, this deprecated gravitational metric unit equals exactly 9.80665 newtons — the weight of a one-thousand-gram mass under standard gravity. What is it?
Kilogram-force (kgf or kgF), or kilopond (kp, from Latin pondus, 'weight'), is a non-standard gravitational metric unit of force equal to the weight on Earth of a one-kilogram mass.
Sometimes a side effect of medication or an alcohol interaction, which state of sluggishness and low motivation usually resolves with rest and better nutrition?
Lethargy is a state of physical or mental weariness, fatigue, sluggishness, or lack of energy.
This paired organ, located near the backbone on either side of the heart in most mammals, extracts oxygen from the air and releases carbon dioxide back into it — name the organ?
Lung are the primary organs of the respiratory system in many animals, including humans.
Often called the 'father of the handheld cell phone,' this Motorola engineer placed the first public mobile call in 1973 from a New York City sidewalk — who is he?
Martin Cooper (inventor) (born December 26, 1928) is an American engineer.

Credited with discovering both the atmosphere of Venus and the law of conservation of mass in chemical reactions, this Russian polymath was also a poet who helped shape the modern Russian literary language and is considered a founder of modern geology — who is he?
Diagnosed after a speech assessment, this condition can stem from psychological trauma or a neurological disorder and isn't always permanent — what is it called?
Muteness is defined as an absence of speech, with or without an ability to hear the speech of others.
Element 102 honors the inventor of dynamite, and its short-lived isotope 255 — with a 3-minute half-life — is the one chemists actually prefer to work with. Which synthetic actinide is it?
Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol No and atomic number 102.

This group of middle-ear inflammations includes a painful acute infection that makes young children tug at their ears, plus a quieter form defined by non-infectious fluid lingering for weeks. What is the condition?
Otitis media is a group of inflammatory diseases of the middle ear.

This psychiatric disorder describes an adult's primary or exclusive sexual attraction to children who haven't yet reached puberty, with diagnostic criteria extending the age cutoff to 13 — what is it called?
Pedophilia (alternatively spelled paedophilia) is a psychiatric disorder in which an adult or older adolescent experiences a primary or exclusive sexual attraction to prepubescent children.
This French physicist shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife, making them the first married couple ever to win a Nobel — who is he?
Pierre Curie (15 May 1859 - 19 April 1906) was a French physicist and chemist, and a pioneer in crystallography and magnetism.
A purplish-black salt that dissolves into an intensely pink-to-purple solution, this strong oxidizer doubles as a WHO-listed medicine for cleaning wounds and dermatitis — what is it?
Potassium permanganate is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula KMnO4.
A polyphenol from the flavonoid family with a naturally bitter taste, this compound turns up in capers and red onions and gets added to supplements — what is it?
Quercetin is a plant flavonol from the flavonoid group of polyphenols.

Winner of the 1905 Nobel Prize for his work on tuberculosis, this German physician identified the causative agents of tuberculosis, cholera, and anthrax, earning him the nickname 'father of microbiology' alongside Louis Pasteur — name this scientist?
Robert Koch (KOKH; 11 December 1843 - 27 May 1910) was a German physician and microbiologist.

Often striking suddenly after heavy lifting and described as a shooting pain down one leg, about 90% of cases trace to a spinal disc herniation pressing on a nerve root — what's this condition called?
Sciatica is pain going down the leg from the lower back.
This small, wingless, primitive insect takes its name from its silvery grey color and darting, fish-like movements — and its scientific name hints at a diet of sugars and starches. What is it?
Silverfish (Lepisma saccharinum) is a species of small, primitive, wingless insect in the order Zygentoma (formerly Thysanura).
Defined as exactly 101,325 pascals and roughly equal to Earth's average sea-level air pressure, what is this reference unit of pressure called?
Standard atmosphere (unit) (symbol: atm) is a unit of pressure defined as 101325 Pa.
This Polish far-right entrepreneur and tax advisor placed third in the 2025 presidential election while chairing a libertarian party and co-leading a far-right coalition — who is he?
Sławomir Mentzen (born 20 November 1986) is a Polish far-right politician, entrepreneur and tax advisor.
Known in medical Latin as the pollex, this digit sits outermost on the hand when you stand palms-forward — which body part?
Thumb is the first digit of the hand, next to the index finger.

This flowering plant in the ginger family is native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, requiring temperatures between 68 and 86°F and high rainfall. Its rhizomes are gathered and can be used fresh or dried for consumption and dyeing — what is it?
Turmeric is a flowering plant in the ginger family Zingiberaceae. Turmeric powder has a warm, bitter, black pepper-like flavor and earthy, mustard-like aroma.
This pungent Japanese condiment, ground from the rhizome of a plant related to horseradish and mustard, traditionally accompanies sushi. What is it?
A white, water-insoluble powder with the formula ZnO, this compound turns up in everything from sunscreens and calamine lotion to batteries and semiconductors — name this compound?
Zinc oxide is an inorganic compound with the formula ZnO. Although it occurs naturally as the mineral zincite, most zinc oxide is produced synthetically.
Made by the adrenal glands, this hormone powers the fight-or-flight response — boosting blood flow to muscles, dilating pupils and raising blood sugar by hitting alpha and beta receptors. What is it?
Adrenaline: Hormone and medication. It appears as a white microcrystalline granule.
Called lucerne in the UK, Australia and New Zealand, this perennial legume has been grown as livestock fodder since ancient times — which plant?
Alfalfa: Plant species in pea family.
A member of the aminopenicillin class, this oral antibiotic is a go-to for ear infections, strep throat, and pneumonia — and is often paired with clavulanic acid. What is it?
NATO codenamed 'Cub,' this four-engine Soviet turboprop served for three decades as the standard cargo and paratroop transport of the Soviet Air Forces — which aircraft?
Antonov An-12: Soviet medium-range transport aircraft.
This order of even-toed hoofed mammals turns out to include whales and dolphins, molecular biology having revealed their close kinship to hippos — what order is it?
Artiodactyla: Order of mammals. Artiodactyla ( AR-tee-oh-DAK-tih-lə; from Ancient Greek ἄρτιος ártios 'even' and δάκτυλος dáktylos 'finger, toe') is an order of placental mammals.

Among the first life forms on Earth and typically just a few micrometres long, these single-celled prokaryotes thrive everywhere from hot springs to radioactive waste and drive the putrefaction stage of decay — what are they?

This steel-gray, brittle alkaline earth metal is found naturally only in combination with other elements, making up gemstones like aquamarine and emerald, and bonds so strongly to oxygen that extracting it is notoriously difficult — which element, atomic number 4?
Beryllium: Chemical element with atomic number 4 (Be)
Conceived for Pan Am as a jet two-and-a-half times the size of the 707, this wide-body, led by designer Joe Sutter, rolled out of the world's largest building in 1968 — which airliner is it?
Boeing 747: American wide-body four-engined jet long-range aircraft.
Often called a 'chest cold,' this inflammation of the airways typically causes a cough lasting around three weeks and is usually caused by a virus?
Bronchitis: Inflammation of the large airways in the lungs.
Originally defined as the heat needed to raise one milliliter of water by one degree Celsius, this unit of energy in nutrition actually refers to a kilocalorie — what is it?

Calorie: Unit of energy used in nutrition. The small calorie or gram calorie is defined as the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of one milliliter of water by one degree Celsius (or one kelvin).
Blending science, aesthetics, and technique, this discipline wrestles with projecting a round world onto flat media while deciding what details to keep or cut — what is it called?
Cartography: Study and practice of making maps.
Beyond the resistance-measuring "bridge" that carries his name, this English inventor also gave us the stereoscope, the English concertina, and the Playfair cipher — who was he?
Charles Wheatstone: English physicist and inventor (1802–1875)

Unlike oysters and mussels, which attach to a surface, or scallops, which live near the bottom, this bivalve mollusk instead burrows into sand or mud on the sea floor — what is it, the namesake of a popular chowder?
Clam: Common name for several kinds of bivalve mollusc.

This medium-sized bird of prey ranges across Europe into northwestern China, hunting rodents like voles from a perch, with northern populations migrating as far as South Africa for winter — what bird is this?
Common buzzard: Species of bird of prey. It is a member of the genus Buteo in the family Accipitridae.
Domesticated in Africa and thriving in sandy, low-rainfall soil, this ancient legume is now grown mostly in Nigeria and Niger, which together supply two-thirds of the world's crop — which plant?
Cowpea: Species of plant. The cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) is an annual herbaceous legume from the genus Vigna.
Son of a bass-baritone and born into a family of engineers, this American built his first car at 19, won four F1 Grands Prix, and took Le Mans in 1967 — who was he?
Dan Gurney: American racing driver, engineer and motorsport executive (1931–2018)
Nicknamed 'dumb cane' because its poisonous sap can temporarily rob you of speech, this shade-tolerant tropical houseplant is native to the New World — which genus?
Dieffenbachia: Genus of plants. Dieffenbachia, commonly known as dumb cane or leopard lily, is a genus of tropical flowering plants in the family Araceae.
This plant genus in the mallow family produces the world's most famously pungent fruit, alongside eight other edible-fruit-bearing species — which genus?
Durio: Genus of plants. Several species produce an edible fruit known as durian, the most common species being Durio zibethinus, with eight others producing edible fruit.
A Swedish scientist and inventor until, at 53, dreams and visions sent him into a spiritual phase, this polymath became best known for his 1758 book on the afterlife, Heaven and Hell — who was he?
Emanuel Swedenborg: Swedish scientist, philosopher, and theologian (1688–1772)
With a sweet smell like pear drops, this colorless solvent turns up in nail-polish remover and is used to decaffeinate tea and coffee. What is it?
First described from a skull in 1846 and initially mistaken for a porpoise, this highly social oceanic dolphin gets its common name from a skull resembling that of the orca — which species?
False killer whale: Species of oceanic dolphin in the genus Pseudorca.
Discovered in Dubna in 1999, this superheavy synthetic element (number 114) honors a Russian physicist whose name in Cyrillic explains why its spelling swaps a 'yo' for an 'e' — which element?
Flerovium: Chemical element with atomic number 114 (Fl)
This Canadian physician and author has written five books linking childhood trauma to conditions like ADHD and addiction, though critics question the evidence behind some claims — who is he?
Known only from teeth and four jawbones, this extinct genus of giant ape roamed China for nearly two million years and is now thought to be a close relative of the orangutan — what is it?
Gigantopithecus: Extinct genus of primate. The species may have been sexually dimorphic, with males much bigger than females.

Native from Mexico down to southern Brazil, this large arboreal lizard can grow past six feet long, is a popular but demanding pet, and has become invasive in many warm regions worldwide — which species?
Green iguana: Species of reptile. Usually, this animal is simply called the iguana.

Named after a bird of prey, this British-developed attack aircraft was the only truly successful vertical-takeoff design of its era, able to fly from car parks and forest clearings instead of vulnerable airbases — which aircraft?
Harrier jump jet: Multirole combat aircraft family by Hawker Siddeley, later British Aerospace.

A Greek physician and philosopher of the classical era, this figure is hailed as the "Father of Medicine" for championing prognosis, clinical observation, and the now-discredited theory of bodily humors — who is he?
Hippocrates: Ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE)
Though phylogenetically closer to cats, these African carnivores resemble dogs thanks to convergent evolution, and their family has just four living species — what animal is it?
This probability principle holds that a randomly typing creature, given endless time, would almost surely reproduce the complete works of Shakespeare — what's it called?
Infinite monkey theorem: Counterintuitive result in probability.

A Manhattan Project veteran, this American physicist won a share of the 1975 Nobel Prize for proposing that not all atomic nuclei are spherical — an idea later confirmed by Aage Bohr and Ben Mottelson. Who was he?
James Rainwater: American physicist. Rainwater joined the physics faculty at Columbia in 1946, where he reached the rank of full professor in 1952 and was named Pupin Professor of Physics in 1982.
Dubbed the 'Angel of Death,' this German physician held doctorates in both anthropology and medicine before joining the SS and selecting Auschwitz prisoners for the gas chambers — who was he?
Josef Mengele: Nazi SS doctor at Auschwitz (1911–1979)
Made from shredded pastry dough layered with cheese and soaked in sugar syrup, this Arab dessert is especially popular during Ramadan, with a famous variant hailing from Nablus — what is it?
Formulated in 1834, this principle of electromagnetism states that an induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the very change in magnetic field that created it — which principle?
Lenz's law: Electromagnetic opposition to change.

Providing the USAF with intercontinental strategic airlift for oversized cargo, this jumbo transport is among the largest military aircraft ever built and shares lineage with the smaller Starlifter — what is it?
Lockheed C-5 Galaxy: American heavy military transport aircraft.
This marsupial family native to Australia and New Guinea includes kangaroos, wallabies, and the quokka among its 63 recognized species — what is it?
Macropodidae: Family of marsupial mammals. Macropodidae is a family of marsupials that includes kangaroos, wallabies, tree-kangaroos, wallaroos, pademelons, the quokka, and several other groups.
A Zainichi Korean entrepreneur, this founder and CEO of SoftBank turned a $20 million bet on Alibaba in 2000 into a stake worth around $75 billion — who is he?
Developed in 1955 and later sold under the brand name Dianabol, this anabolic steroid was once widely used for physique and performance enhancement — what is it?
Metandienone: Androgen and anabolic steroid. It is also used non-medically for physique- and performance-enhancing purposes.

Prized for their fur and related to weasels and otters, these semiaquatic carnivores have established wild populations in Britain and Denmark after farm escapes and animal-rights releases — what are they?
Mink: Mammal in the family Mustelidae.
This contagious, vaccine-preventable viral disease is best known for causing painful swelling of the glands beside the jaw — its hallmark symptom. What is it?
Mumps: Human disease caused by paramyxovirus.
Discovered in 1885 by Carl Auer von Welsbach, this rare-earth element tarnishes quickly in air and produces pink, purple, and yellow compounds when oxidized — which element, atomic number 60?
Neodymium: Chemical element with atomic number 60 (Nd)
This facial organ houses the nares, connects to the humidity-regulating paranasal sinuses, and serves as an alternate airway for nursing infants — which body part?
Nose: Organ that smells and facilitates breathing.
First domesticated in China's Yangtze River basin more than 8,000 years ago, this grass species is the world's most widely cultivated rice — which species?
Oryza sativa: Species of plant. Oryza sativa belongs to the genus Oryza and the BOP clade in the grass family Poaceae.
Defined as the distance at which one astronomical unit subtends an angle of one arcsecond, this unit equals about 3.26 light-years — which unit?
Parsec: Unit of length in astronomy.
Featuring an R−O−O−R backbone where two oxygen atoms bond directly to each other, what name covers this class of molecules?
Peroxide: Chemical compounds with the structure R–O–O–R'
Resembling a round, tailless rabbit with short ears, this small mountain-dwelling mammal's Himalayan relative lives at elevations above 6,000 meters — what animal is it?
Pika: Genus of mountain-dwelling mammal. A pika ( PY-kə, PEE-kə) is a small, mountain-dwelling mammal native to Asia and North America.
This succulent plant in the family Portulacaceae has every part edible, whether raw or cooked, and is also known by folk names like little hogweed — what is it, scientifically speaking?
Portulaca oleracea: Species of plant in the purslane family.

This noncontagious autoimmune disease shows up as dry, scaly red or purple patches, and injuring the skin can trigger new lesions right at that spot — a quirk called the Koebner phenomenon — what is it?
Psoriasis: Autoimmune diseases of the skin. Psoriasis is a long-lasting, noncontagious autoimmune disease characterized by patches of abnormal skin.

Born Richard Alpert, this spiritual teacher researched psychedelics with Timothy Leary at Harvard before writing the 1971 bestseller Be Here Now, popularizing Eastern spirituality in the West. What name did he later take?
This English anatomist coined the word 'Dinosauria' — 'terrible reptile' — yet remained an outspoken critic of Darwin's theory of natural selection — who is it?
Richard Owen: English biologist and palaeontologist (1804–1892)
Also known as brewer's or baker's yeast, this single-celled fungus believed to have originated on grape skins is one of biology's most-studied model organisms — which species?
Saccharomyces cerevisiae: Species of yeast. The species has been instrumental in winemaking, baking, and brewing since ancient times.
Comprising seven species from the flatback to the leatherback, five of these ocean-dwelling reptiles are threatened with extinction — what are they?
Sea turtle: Reptiles of the superfamily Chelonioidea.
Highly water-soluble and non-hygroscopic, this colorless compound with formula AgNO3 is the least expensive salt of its kind — which compound?
Silver nitrate: Chemical compound. It is highly water soluble colorless solid that is a precursor to many other silver compounds.
Combining vowel and consonant sounds into words for acts like persuading or declaring, this use of the human voice can even happen without any listener at all — what is it?
Speech: Human vocal communication using spoken language.

Caused by blocked or bleeding blood flow to the brain, this medical emergency can cause facial drooping and one-sided weakness — and if symptoms fade within a day, it's called a 'mini' version instead. What is this condition?
Stroke: Death of a region of brain cells due to poor blood flow.
Turkey's only female prime minister to date, this economist-turned-politician led the country from 1993 to 1996 as head of the True Path Party — who is she?
Tansu Çiller: Prime Minister of Turkey from 1993 to 1996. As a professor of economics, Çiller was appointed Minister of State for the economy by Prime Minister Süleyman Demirel in 1991.
One of the three great clades of dinosaur, its members share hollow bones and three clawed toes per limb, were ancestrally carnivorous, and likely wore feathers in the Coelurosauria — which group?

Once dismissed as rare and bizarre, this childhood-onset disorder pairs multiple motor tics with at least one vocal tic, often heralded by a premonitory urge the person can briefly suppress — what's it called?
Tourette syndrome: Neurodevelopmental disorder involving motor and vocal tics.
Often caused by poor circulation or prolonged pressure on the skin, this open sore — also known as a bedsore when linked to immobility — can destroy tissue down to the fat layer. What is it called?

The northernmost marsupial on Earth, this cat-sized nocturnal opportunist is a familiar visitor to trash cans and compost piles across North America, and often ends up as roadkill due to its slow pace — what is it?
Virginia opossum: Species of North American marsupial.
